The Math
Basic Concept: Meals x Rate = Money
At its core, the equation is the number of qualifying meals served, multiplied by the
government's reimbursement rate for each meal type, equals the dollar amount the federal
government pays the school or program.
Meals Served  ×  Reimbursement Rate  =  Federal Payment
The federal government doesn't pay schools directly. USDA pays the state agency (like a state
Department of Education), and the state pays the school districts. The math happens at every
level of that chain.
Eligibility Categories
Not every meal is reimbursed at the same rate. USDA pays more for meals served to children
from lower-income households. There are three categories, and each has its own rate.
The Full Rate Table (SY2026-27)

Meal Type Free Reduced Paid Notes
<!-- page: 2 -->
Example:
Lincoln Elementary serves 420 lunches in October 2025:
295 Free meals  ×  $4.28  =  $1,262.60
52 Reduced meals  ×  $3.97  =  $206.44
73 Paid meals  ×  $0.53  =  $38.69
Total federal reimbursement for October: $1,507.73
How does the system know which children are Free vs. Reduced?
1. Families submit a household income application. A staff member reviews it and assigns the
category.
2. The state runs an overnight match against SNAP and Medicaid records. Children who match
are automatically certified Free without any application at all. This is called Direct Certification.
Locking in Rates
Here's a problem the system has to solve: USDA publishes new reimbursement rates every July
1. What happens to a claim that was submitted before July 1 but gets revised after July 1? Should
it use the old rate or the new rate?
The answer is: always the rate for the original claim month. A revised claim for October 2024
processed in August 2025 uses the October 2024 rate — not the August 2025 rate. This is true
even if the school year's rates have since been updated.
The system enforces this through a mechanism called ClaimLaws. When a school's application
is approved, ClaimLaws records the school's eligibility tier — whether the school qualifies for
the severe-need rate, which meal groups apply, and their operating parameters. Dollar amounts
are not stored in ClaimLaws.

<!-- page: 3 -->
When a claim is computed, the system looks up the eligibility tier from ClaimLaws, then retrieves
the corresponding dollar amounts from the rate table using the original claim month as the key.
Because rates are indexed by date, a December 2024 claim always resolves to the December
2024 rate — even if it is revised or reprocessed after new rates have been published.
Before ClaimLaws existed, a rate update in July would silently change the reimbursement on 
every prior-year revised claim that got reprocessed. A school district disputing a claim from
October 2024 would suddenly find their revised claim being recalculated at the July 2025 rate
— which is wrong. ClaimLaws makes this structurally impossible.
What ClaimLaws stores: the eligibility tier (standard vs. severe need), the applicable meal
groups, operating parameters, and the effective date range. This is the school-specific
determination made at application approval time. The dollar amounts that correspond to that tier
for any given claim month are looked up separately at compute time — keeping rate updates a
simple data operation that never touches approved applications.
Community Eligibility Provision (CEP)
Collecting individual household income applications is a lot of work — for families, for school
staff, and for state agencies. In high-poverty schools where almost everyone qualifies anyway, it
creates paperwork for little benefit. The Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) solves this by
letting qualifying schools skip individual applications entirely and serve all students free meals.
But the federal government still needs to know what to pay. They can't just pay the free meal
rate for every meal — not every student at a CEP school is actually from a low-income
household. So USDA created a formula that estimates the right reimbursement based on how
many students are directly certified (automatically verified through SNAP, Medicaid, etc.)
without requiring individual applications.

<!-- page: 4 -->
The ISP Formula
ISP = Identified Students ÷ Total Enrollment × 100
The Identified Student Percentage (ISP) is the share of enrolled students who are directly
certified through a government benefit program. A school with 300 students where 180 are
directly certified has an ISP of 60%.
To qualify for CEP, the ISP must be at least 40%.
The Claiming Percentage Formula
Claiming % = ISP × 1.6  (capped at 100%)
USDA multiplies the ISP by 1.6 to produce the Claiming Percentage — the share of all meals
reimbursed at the free rate. The multiplier of 1.6 is set by federal regulation and cannot be
changed.
CEP Groups
A school district doesn't have to elect CEP school-by-school. They can pool schools into a CEP
Group, combining all those schools' enrollment and identified students into one ISP calculation.
This helps schools that are just under the 40% threshold by averaging them with higher-
qualifying schools in the same group.
Example 
Salt Lake City SD has three west-side schools. Individually, two qualify but one doesn't:
Lincoln Elementary: 295/412 students identified = 71.6% ISP ✓
Roosevelt Elementary: 180/380 students identified = 47.4% ISP ✓
Jefferson Elementary: 140/410 students identified = 34.1% ISP ✗  (below 40%)
Pooled as a group: 615 identified ÷ 1,202 enrolled = 51.2% ISP → 81.9% Claiming %. All three
schools join CEP together.

<!-- page: 5 -->
The 1.6 multiplier is federal law. It cannot be configured The system must not allow any state-
specific override of this multiplier. It is set in 42 U.S.C. § 1759a(a)(1)(F)(viii). Any attempt to make
it configurable would constitute a federal compliance violation.
Provision 2 & 3: Schools That Don't Count Applications Every Year
Before CEP existed, USDA offered two older programs for high-poverty schools to reduce
paperwork. Both are still in use today.
Provision 2
Under Provision 2, a school establishes a base year by collecting full household income
applications once, measuring the percentage of Free/Reduced/Paid meals accurately. For the
next three years (the non-base years), the school claims using those same percentages — they
don't collect new applications or recount eligibility. They just report total meals served and the
system applies the base-year percentages.
Provision 2 Math
Base year established: 68% Free, 12% Reduced, 20% Paid.
In Year 3, Provo serves 22,840 total lunches in September:
22,840 × 68% = 15,531 Free meals × $4.28 = $66,472.68
22,840 × 12% = 2,741 Reduced meals × $3.97 = $10,881.77
22,840 × 20% = 4,568 Paid meals × $0.53 = $2,421.04
Total: $79,775.49 — calculated from base-year percentages, not individual eligibility records.
Provision 3
Provision 3 also eliminates annual application collection, but its mechanism is different from
Provision 2. Rather than simply applying base-year percentages to reported meal counts,
Provision 3 captures richer base-year data — including claiming percentages (share of total
meals that were Free, Reduced, and Paid) and eligibility percentages (share of enrolled

<!-- page: 6 -->
students in each category) — and uses those ratios to project non-base year meals from
enrollment and operating days alone.
In a non-base year, the sponsor enters only two values: current enrollment and number of
operating days. The system then:
1. Scales the base-year total meal count proportionally for enrollment change and operating
days
2. Applies base-year claiming percentages to get the Free/Reduced/Paid breakdown
3. Feeds those counts into the standard reimbursement calculation at current USDA rates
There is no separate inflation adjustment — current rates apply automatically through the
normal annual rate update process, the same as any other claim. The goal is administrative
simplification: eliminating annual application collection at high-poverty schools where eligibility
is high and stable. Far less common than Provision 2.
When a Provision 2 or 3 school is found to have overclaimed, the state agency can't simply
compare meal counts against individual eligibility records because those records don't exist for
non-base years. USDA requires a different fiscal action formula (FA2 or FA3) specifically for
Provision schools. This is why the compliance system has four separate fiscal workbook
variants.
CACFP: Daycare and After-School Programs
Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) works on the same Meals × Rate = Money
principle as school programs, but the rate structure is different. In CACFP, the rate you receive
depends on the type of provider, not just the child's income level.
Two Tiers of Providers
CACFP day care homes (individual home-based childcare providers) are divided into two tiers
based on the provider's own income or the income level of the neighborhood where they
operate.

<!-- page: 7 -->
Meal Patterns Are Different
CACFP also has stricter meal pattern requirements than school programs. A CACFP breakfast
must include a grain, a milk, and a fruit or vegetable. A lunch must include a meat/meat
alternate, a grain, two different vegetables or fruits, and milk. The system checks that claimed
meals meet the pattern — meals that don't meet the pattern are disallowed even if the count is
otherwise correct.
Meal Limits Per Day
CACFP day care homes can claim a maximum of two meals and one snack per child per day, or
one meal and two snacks per child per day. A child cannot be claimed for three full meals. This
cap is enforced in the claim validation logic.
Centers vs. Homes
CACFP covers both institutional centers (a licensed daycare facility) and individual home-based
providers (someone running daycare from their house). Centers claim at a single rate based on
enrolled children's individual eligibility. Homes use the Tier I/II system. The claims data model
handles these separately.
SFSP & SSFO
Summer meal programs are designed to be simpler than school-year programs. Instead of
tracking individual children's eligibility, summer programs operate as open sites where any child
18 or under who shows up eats for free. No applications. No eligibility sorting. No
Free/Reduced/Paid categories.
Because all meals are free, there's only one reimbursement rate per meal type.
The Attendance Requirement
Summer programs can only claim meals for children who are actually present. Unlike schools
that can project meal counts, SFSP sites must record actual attendance. The system enforces a 
50% attendance cap at some site types — you can't claim more meals than half the enrolled
capacity if actual attendance records aren't available.

<!-- page: 8 -->
Non-Congregate Meals (SFSP)
Traditional summer meal rules require children to eat together at the site — called congregate
service. After COVID, USDA permanently allowed some sites to offer non-congregate meals:
grab-and-go bags, parent pick-up, or delivery to children who can't reach the site. Non-
congregate service has stricter recordkeeping requirements and the system enforces three
distinct modes:
Congregate only — children eat at the site, standard rules apply
Non-congregate only — all meals are distributed for off-site consumption
Mixed — some meals eaten on-site, some distributed; each must be tracked separately
SSFO — Seamless Summer Food Option
Some schools want to keep serving meals through summer without switching from their NSLP
paperwork to SFSP paperwork. The Seamless Summer Food Option (SSFO) lets them operate
under school-year administrative rules but with summer funding. Their reimbursement rates are
similar to NSLP but come from a different federal grant account. The system keeps SSFO claims
separate from both NSLP and SFSP claims to prevent the different rules from mixing.
Why SFSP rates are higher per meal than NSLP free ratesSFSP is fully federally funded —
states and local programs receive no additional state funds or family copayments. The higher
per-meal rate compensates for the lack of other funding sources and the higher administrative
cost of summer-only operations.
FFVP: Allocation Math
The USDA gives each selected school a fixed dollar amount for the year based on their
enrollment, and the school spends that money on fresh produce served as snacks. USDA sets
the per-student amount each school year (approximately $50–$75 per student). Only high-
poverty elementary schools are eligible, typically those with 50%+ free and reduced eligibility,
and selection is by state agency invitation, not application.
Annual Allocation = Enrolled Students × Per-Student Amount

<!-- page: 9 -->
No ClaimLaws needed for FFVPBecause FFVP reimbursement equals actual expenditure rather
than meals × rate, there's no reimbursement rate to freeze. The school is simply reimbursed for
what they spent, up to their allocation cap.
Fiscal Action Math
When a state agency reviews a school or program and finds that they claimed more meals than
they actually served or claimed meals that didn't meet the program requirements the state must
calculate how much money needs to be paid back. This is called a fiscal action.
USDA requires specific formulas depending on what type of school is being reviewed. There are
four variants, called FA1 through FA4.
The Five-Day Reconciliation (The Most Common Finding Source)
During an on-site review, the reviewer doesn't examine every single day of a school year.
Instead, they pick a sample — usually five days from a recent month's claim. They compare the
number of meals the kitchen produced on each of those days against the number the school 
claimed on each of those days. If there's a gap, they extrapolate it across the full year.
Five-Day Reconciliation + FA2 — Provo City Schools (Provision 2 School)
Reviewer samples 5 days from September 2025. Total gap found: 312 meals over 5 days.
September had 21 operating days. FA2 formula:
The $5,305.50 moves to the Accounting domain as a repayment schedule. Provo's next
disbursement is reduced by that amount.
The calculation of how much is owed is an enforcement function living with the review record. 
The collection of what's owed (the repayment schedule, the check received) lives in
Accounting. Accounting only receives the final dollar number. It never needs to know whether
1 312 meals ÷ 5 sample days × 21 operating days = 1,310 estimated overclaimed meals
2 1,310 × $4.05 blended rate = $5,305.50 assessed repayment
<!-- page: 10 -->
FA1, FA2, FA3, or FA4 was used.
Annual Rate Updates:
Every July 1, USDA publishes new reimbursement rates for the upcoming school year. In the old
architecture, applying these new rates meant updating stored procedures, redeploying code to
each state, and hoping nothing broke. In the new architecture, it's a single database INSERT
that takes effect for all states simultaneously — no code changes, no deployments.
Three Types of Annual Federal Changes
The Type 1 Rate Update in Detail
In DIS and CTS, reimbursement rates are often embedded in stored procedure logic, not in a
table. A rate change means finding every SP that referenced the old rate, updating each one,
testing, and deploying per state. The new design makes rates data, not code.
Anomaly Gate
USDA occasionally publishes corrections and has issued erroneous rate documents before. The
system flags any rate increase or decrease greater than 10% from the prior year for mandatory
human review before the INSERT is allowed. A 3–4% annual increase is normal (inflation

<!-- page: 11 -->
adjustment). A 15% jump would be suspicious and must be confirmed against the official
Federal Register document before going in.
